To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) The energy supply and demand of livestock on the farmlets was estimated from regular measurements of the feed energy supply and demand, respectively, and (2) the energy supplied was at times inadequate for the energy demands of livestock on all three farmlets suggesting that the farmlets were overstocked.

the energy supplied in pasture and supplements was generally adequate to meet the energy demand of grazing livestock on three farmlets, but that the energy supplied during winter was often inadequate to meet demand.
the energy balance of the farmlets was generally negative during the winter period, with a greater deficit occurring on farmlet C.
In summary, our research is concerned with
developing a better understanding of the balance between the supply and demand of pasture feed energy in grazing systems.
the development of a practical, cost-effective and accurate method for estimating the balance between pasture supply and demand of energy from grazing livestock.
developing methods to quantify the balance of feed supply and demand for grazing livestock in a pasture-based farming system.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, in the case of these three farmlets, the feed supply and demand were in balance, but that there was a need for greater flexibility of management in the timing of grazing events.
, in the absence of any other information, the energy supply and demand of the farmlets was balanced.

the three differently managed systems of grazing management were over stocked and that there was a need to reduce the level of stocking rate on all three farmlets to achieve a positive partial energy balance over winter.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

it was a good example of a well designed and executed farmlet study that has provided valuable insights into the potential to improve livestock production through better management of pasture feed resources.

the Cicerone experiment was able to provide an estimate, albeit partial, of the net feed energy balance between feed supply (pasture growth and supplementation) and demand (livestock energy requirements) over a 6.5-year period.

the Cicerone experiment has demonstrated how the energy supply from pasture and supplementation and the energy demand from livestock can be quantified and monitored in a farmlet setting, thereby providing a means of identifying the balance between feed energy supply and livestock demand and the potential for improved grazing management to improve this balance.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the balance between feed energy supply and demand can be estimated using a combination of satellite imagery and livestock management data.

the energy balance of grazing livestock can be estimated from readily available data and used to identify periods when the feed energy supply is inadequate to satisfy the energy requirements of the livestock.

there is considerable scope for improvement in the management of grazing livestock on farms in the region, if the energy balance between pasture feed and livestock can be monitored more regularly and the results used to adjust the stocking rate and the timing and level of supplementary feed fed.
